name: Vajrayāna (Mantranaya) in India
alt_names: Zhenyan / Mizong (Chinese, for the early stream)

tradition.text: taught by the Buddha in the form of Vajradhara (e.g. the Kālacakra at Dhānyakaṭaka, the Guhyasamāja to King Indrabhūti of Oḍḍiyāna); hidden and revealed to qualified disciples

scholarly.text: c. 6th–13th c. CE in India: kriyā/caryā texts from the 6th c. (dhāraṇī literature earlier); Mahāvairocana mid-7th c.; Tattvasaṃgraha late 7th c.; Guhyasamāja c. 8th c.; Yoginī tantras c. 9th–10th c.; Kālacakra early 11th c. (epoch 1027); decline after c. 1200

transmissions_received.what: the bodhisattva path, the six perfections and the goal of buddhahood for all beings
transmissions_received.evidence: the tantras present themselves as Mahāyāna (the mantra method within the Mahāyāna)

transmissions_received.what: emptiness as the view of the tantras (Ārya Guhyasamāja exegesis; Advayavajra)
transmissions_received.evidence: Pañcakrama and Advayavajrasaṃgraha frame the stages in Madhyamaka terms

transmissions_received.what: mind-only and the four gnoses (mirror-like etc.) mapped to the five buddha families
transmissions_received.evidence: the five gnoses (Yogācāra's four plus dharmadhātu gnosis)

transmissions_received.what: ritual technology (maṇḍala, homa, nyāsa), pīṭha lists and the cremation-ground idiom of the Yoginī tantras

distinctive_positions: Buddhahood can be attained in this very life and body (Pañcakrama 3.12; the 'swift path'), by the Mahāyāna view joined with special methods (deity yoga, mantra, the subtle body).

The mantra method is superior to the perfection method in being unconfused, rich in means, not difficult and for those of sharp faculties (Tripiṭakamala's Nayatrayapradīpa, the classic Indian statement).
Entry requires consecration (abhiṣeka) from a qualified vajra master and keeping the pledges (samaya); the teacher is to be regarded as inseparable from Vajradhara (Gurupañcāśikā 22).

The path has two stages: generation (utpattikrama) — the practitioner arises as the deity in the maṇḍala — and completion (utpanna-/niṣpannakrama) — work with channels, winds and drops toward clear light and union.
The passions are not only abandoned but used as the path ('poison as medicine'); desire in particular is transformed into great bliss (mahāsukha) joined with emptiness.
The goal is the union (yuganaddha) of clear light and illusory body, or of immutable bliss and empty form (Kālacakra), the non-duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Tantric statements are coded ('intentional language', sandhyābhāṣā) and must be read with the explanatory tantras and the guru's instruction (the six alternatives, ṣaṭkoṭi).
summary: The esoteric Mahāyāna of India that teaches the swift path to buddhahood by mantra, deity yoga in the maṇḍala, consecration by a vajra master and the yogas of the subtle body, codified in tantras revealed (by the tradition's account) by the Buddha as Vajradhara and, historically, composed c. 6th–11th c. and taught at Nālandā, Vikramaśīla and among the wandering siddhas; transmitted to Tibet, Nepal and East Asia.

name: The Mahāsiddhas (the eighty-four great adepts)

tradition.text: Saraha, 'the great brahmin', counted first of the human teachers of mahāmudrā; the siddhas lived long lives, some for centuries (Nāgārjuna), and some are said not to have died

scholarly.text: c. 8th–12th c. CE; Abhayadatta's collection of lives c. 11th–12th c.

transmissions_received.what: the tantras (esp. Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara, Guhyasamāja) and their empowerments
transmissions_received.evidence: the lives name the tantra and instruction each siddha received

transmissions_given.what: Saraha's and Tilopa's mahāmudrā, Nāropa's six yogas, the dohā-song idiom (mgur)
Virūpa's Path and Result (lam 'bras) based on the Hevajra
Niguma's and Sukhasiddhi's instructions
Ghaṇṭāpa's, Lūipa's and Kāṇha's Cakrasaṃvara and Nāropa's Vajrayoginī
shared siddha names and songs (disputed direction; see brw:natha-mahasiddha)
sahaja as the goal, body-cosmology (disputed; see brw:mahasiddha-to-vaisnava-sahajiya)

distinctive_positions: The innate (sahaja), the nature of one's own mind, is the ultimate; it is found not by learning, ritual or contrived meditation but through the true guru's instruction (People Dohā v19, v38–39).
Brahmanical, Jain and Buddhist monastic observances and even tantric ritual are criticized when taken as ends in themselves (People Dohā v2–15; Queen Dohā v32).
Realization is lived in ordinary life — householder, courtesan, weaver, cobbler, fisherman, king — and each siddha's own trade becomes the image of the path (Caturaśītisiddhabodhihṛdaya).
The songs (dohā, caryā) use intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā): outer images for inner yoga.
Unconventional conduct (vratacaryā, unmattacaryā) is undertaken only after realization and with discernment (Caturaśītisiddhabodhihṛdaya: Nāgārjuna's song; Mekopa's song).
summary: The Indian tantric adepts (siddhas) of c. 8th–12th c. — the eighty-four of Abhayadatta's lives and others — whose songs (dohās, caryāgīti) and instructions teach the innate (sahaja) and mahāmudrā beyond ritual and conceptual meditation, and whose lineages passed into the Tibetan Kagyu, Sakya and other schools and overlap with the Nāth siddhas.

name: Ārya tradition of the Guhyasamāja

tradition.text: founded by Nāgārjuna and his disciples Āryadeva, Nāgabodhi and Candrakīrti — identified with the Madhyamaka masters

scholarly.text: the tantric authors c. 9th–10th c., distinct from the Madhyamaka authors of the 2nd–7th c.

transmissions_given.what: the Ārya Guhyasamāja exegesis (Tsongkhapa's Rim lnga gsal sgron)
Marpa's Guhyasamāja from Nāropa

distinctive_positions: The completion stage is five (or six) stages: speech isolation (vajra recitation), mind isolation, self-consecration (illusory body), clear light (abhisambodhi) and union (yuganaddha) (Pañcakrama).
The four empties (śūnya, atiśūnya, mahāśūnya, sarvaśūnya) arise as winds dissolve; the fourth is clear light (Pañcakrama 2.4–5).
The illusory body arisen from wind-and-mind is the conventional truth, clear light the ultimate; their union is buddhahood (Pañcakrama 3.13, 5.11).
The root tantra is coded and must be read through the explanatory tantras (Vajramālā, Sandhivyākaraṇa, Caturdevīparipṛcchā) and the six alternatives (Pradīpoddyotana).
summary: The exegetical school of the Guhyasamāja tantra associated with the tantric Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, Nāgabodhi and Candrakīrti, which systematized the completion stage in five stages leading through the four empties to clear light, illusory body and union; its Akṣobhya-centred 32-deity maṇḍala was taken into Tibet (Marpa, Gö Khukpa Lhetse) and made central by Tsongkhapa.

name: Jñānapāda tradition of the Guhyasamāja

tradition.text: Buddhajñānapāda received the teaching directly from Mañjuśrī after years of practice

transmissions_given.what: the Jñānapāda Guhyasamāja (Mañjuvajra) lineage

distinctive_positions: The Guhyasamāja is practised with Mañjuvajra (a form of Mañjuśrī) at the centre of a 19-deity maṇḍala.
The 'two stages' are presented in Buddhajñānapāda's 'Oral Instruction' (Dvikramatattvabhāvanā-mukhāgama), given, by the tradition's account, by Mañjuśrī himself.
summary: The second Indian exegetical tradition of the Guhyasamāja, founded by Buddhajñānapāda (late 8th c.), a teacher of Vikramaśīla's early masters, centred on Mañjuvajra and the 'Oral Instruction' on the two stages; continued by Dīpaṅkarabhadra's maṇḍala ritual (Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi).
notes: The 19-deity count and the Mukhāgama's reception from Mañjuśrī are recalled, not checked in a text.

name: Cakrasaṃvara (Saṃvara, Heruka) tradition in India
regions: the 24 pīṭhas of the Heruka maṇḍala

tradition.text: Heruka subdued Maheśvara (Bhairava) and his retinue at the twenty-four sites; the tantra is an abridgement of a larger tantra of 100,000 verses

scholarly.text: Laghuśaṃvara c. late 8th–9th c.; explanatory tantras 9th–10th c.

transmissions_given.what: the three Indian lineages (Lūipa, Ghaṇṭāpa, Kāṇha) and the Vajrayoginī cycles
the three Indian lineages (Lūipa, Ghaṇṭāpa, Kāṇha) and the Vajrayoginī cycles

Cakrasaṃvara and Vajravārāhī as the principal esoteric deities

distinctive_positions: Heruka (Cakrasaṃvara) in union with Vajravārāhī is the embodiment of great bliss and emptiness.
The maṇḍala's twenty-four sacred sites (pīṭha etc.) are located in the outer land and, inwardly, in the yogin's body as channels (the body maṇḍala).
Three Indian lineages of practice: Lūipa's (with Vajravārāhī's cycle), Ghaṇṭāpa's (the five-deity body maṇḍala) and Kāṇha's (Kṛṣṇācārya's).
The Vajrayoginī (Vajravārāhī) sādhanas of Nāropa, Indrabhūti and Maitrīpa belong to this cycle.
summary: The Yoginī-tantra tradition centred on Heruka Cakrasaṃvara and Vajravārāhī, based on the Laghuśaṃvara and its explanatory tantras, with the twenty-four sacred sites (shared with Śaiva pīṭha lists) mapped onto the body, and three Indian practice lineages (Lūipa, Ghaṇṭāpa, Kāṇha) that passed to Tibet and the Newars.

name: Kālacakra tradition in India

tradition.text: taught by the Buddha at Dhānyakaṭaka to King Sucandra of Śambhala; abridged by Mañjuśrīyaśas and commented on by Puṇḍarīka (the Vimalaprabhā); brought to India from Śambhala

scholarly.text: Laghukālacakra and Vimalaprabhā composed c. 1025–1040; epoch year 1027 (start of the sixty-year cycle)

transmissions_given.what: the Kālacakra tantra, commentaries, six-branch yoga and calendar
the Kālacakra tantra, commentaries, six-branch yoga and calendar
the Kālacakra tantra, commentaries, six-branch yoga and calendar
the Kālacakra tantra, commentaries, six-branch yoga and calendar

distinctive_positions: The outer (cosmos and time), inner (body, channels, winds) and other/alternative (the deity and maṇḍala) Kālacakras correspond; liberation reverses the flow of time within the body.
The six-branch yoga (pratyāhāra, dhyāna, prāṇāyāma, dhāraṇā, anusmṛti, samādhi) leads through ten signs to empty form (śūnyatābimba) joined with immutable bliss (akṣarasukha) (Sekoddeśa 24–27, 146).
The Ādibuddha, the primordial buddha, is the non-dual gnosis of immutable bliss.
Śambhala's kings will in the future defeat the barbarian (mleccha) religion and restore the dharma (a prophecy in the first chapter).
Its own astronomy and calendar, and a prophecy of the kalkin rulers of Śambhala.
summary: The last major Indian tantric system (11th c.), the 'Wheel of Time', which correlates cosmos, body and deity, teaches the six-branch yoga culminating in empty form and immutable bliss, gives its own astronomy and calendar (epoch 1027) and the Śambhala narrative; taught by Kālacakrapāda, Nāropa and Abhayākaragupta and transmitted to Tibet (Jonang, Gelug, Sakya).
